chapter.title: Linear motion under a variable force

lessons.title: Time-dependent forces and complete trajectories
lessons.summary: Integrate with the initial conditions, then distinguish displacement, distance and a change of model.
lessons.objective: Construct signed velocity and displacement functions and apply them only over their physical time intervals.
lessons.before: Review differentiation, definite integration, exponentials and logarithms. The signed-components lesson explains direction conventions. A force law supplies acceleration only after division by the moving mass.
lessons.ideas:
Three linked quantities, one positive direction

\[\begin{gathered}v=\frac{dx}{dt}\\a=\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}\\F_{\rm resultant}=ma\end{gathered}\]

Displacement and velocity are signed; speed is |v|. A negative acceleration means acceleration in the negative coordinate direction. It reduces speed only while velocity is positive. State the mass and all real force directions before forming the differential equation.

Integrate twice, using two initial conditions

When acceleration is a known function of time, integrate to get v(t), apply the velocity condition, integrate again for x(t), and apply the position condition. If the given relation couples v and x, use v=dx/dt and separate variables when possible.

\[\begin{gathered}v(t)=u+\int_0^t a(s)\,ds\\x(t)=x_0+\int_0^t v(s)\,ds\end{gathered}\]

A constant of integration is not automatically zero because t=0 was chosen. For x′=f(t)x, division by x needs attention to the possible rest-at-zero solution; the nonzero initial state determines the branch used.

Time-dependent factors can make separation possible

An equation v′=f(t)h(v) separates into dv/h(v)=f(t)dt wherever the divisor is nonzero. Check any constant-velocity solution lost by division and then apply the initial condition. Differentiate the proposed answer and check the initial value before using it.

Distance counts both directions

\[\begin{gathered}\Delta x=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}v(t)\,dt\\s=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}|v(t)|\,dt\end{gathered}\]

Locate every velocity zero in the required interval and split the distance integral at each actual reversal. A turning point has v=0; a return to the origin has x=0. They are different events. A force changing sign is not itself proof that velocity changes sign at that time.

A switch starts a new stage

If a finite force is switched off with no impulse, position and velocity remain continuous. Use their values at the switch as the next stage's initial conditions. Do not continue the old acceleration law after its stated cutoff. The resultant work equals the change in kinetic energy even when the force varies.

Limits are not events by themselves

A velocity can stay positive for every finite time while tending to zero. Inspect the displacement function or its integral to decide whether the total distance is finite. A formula with a finite-time pole has a shorter domain than all t≥0, even if it can be evaluated algebraically on another branch.
lessons.method:
1. Choose a positive direction and form the signed resultant-force equation.
  2. Integrate or separate the appropriate differential equation.
  3. Use every initial condition and verify the answer by differentiation.
  4. Find turns, returns and switches in the correct order.
  5. Use absolute velocity for distance and state the interval where the model applies.
mistakes: Divide resultant force by mass before integrating.
Initial position and initial velocity supply separate constants.
Negative acceleration does not always mean decreasing speed.
A turning time does not equal a return time.
A force switched off does not reset velocity to zero.

examples.title: 1 · Both integration constants matter
examples.question: A 3 kg particle has resultant force \(F=6-3t\) N. Initially x=1 m and v=3 m s⁻¹. Find x(t), v(t), and the first non-negative turning time for this model.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}a=2-t\\v=3+2t-\frac12t^2\\x=1+3t+t^2-\frac16t^3\\v=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t=2+\sqrt{10}\end{gathered}\]

The other root is negative. The force is zero at t=2, when velocity is still positive; it is not the turning instant.

examples.title: 2 · A displacement–velocity relation is an ODE
examples.question: A 2 kg particle satisfies \(v/x=3/(t+2)\) for t≥0 and starts at x=8 m. Find its trajectory and resultant force.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\frac1x\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac3{t+2}\\\ln x=3\ln(t+2)+C\\x=(t+2)^3\\v=3(t+2)^2\\F=2\frac{dv}{dt}=12(t+2)\end{gathered}\]

The initial displacement fixes the multiplicative constant at one. The trajectory stays positive, so the division by x is valid on this branch.

examples.title: 3 · Positive velocity with finite total travel
examples.question: A particle starts at O with velocity 9 m s⁻¹ and has acceleration \(-18/(1+t)^3\) m s⁻² for t≥0. Find its displacement and describe its eventual position.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v=\frac9{(1+t)^2}\\x=9\left(1-\frac1{1+t}\right)\\0\le x\lt9,\qquad v\gt0\end{gathered}\]

The particle approaches x=9 m without reaching it at finite time. Its total distance is 9 m because velocity stays positive and the displacement has that finite limit.

examples.title: 4 · A reversal before a force switches off
examples.question: A 2 kg particle starts at O with velocity 4 m s⁻¹. Its resultant force is \(-4t\) N until t=3 s, and zero thereafter. Find distance travelled by t=3, the first return time to O and work done in the first three seconds.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v=4-t^2,\qquad x=4t-\frac13t^3\\t_{\rm turn}=2,\quad x(2)=\frac{16}3\\x(3)=3,\qquad v(3)=-5\\s=2x(2)-x(3)=\frac{23}3\\T=3+\frac35=\frac{18}5\\W=\frac12(2)(25-16)=9\end{gathered}\]

After t=3 the particle moves uniformly leftwards. Extending the earlier cubic trajectory into that stage would give the wrong return time.

lessons.title: Position-dependent force and the physical velocity branch
lessons.summary: Use the chain rule to find v², then select the direction and test whether a candidate point is reachable.
lessons.objective: Link force, velocity and position, including finite-time and asymptotic boundaries.
lessons.before: Complete signed trajectories and initial conditions. Review separable equations, the chain rule and improper integrals. Use a monotone segment when treating velocity as a function of position.
lessons.ideas:
The chain rule changes the independent variable

\[\begin{gathered}\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{dv}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt}=v\frac{dv}{dx}\\\frac12(v^2-u^2)=\int_{x_0}^{x}\frac{F(s)}m\,ds\end{gathered}\]

The integral is also the work–energy relation divided by mass. Do not integrate F/m directly to obtain v when x is the integration variable: the left side is ∫v dv. A constant-force SUVAT formula is inappropriate for a general variable force.

A squared velocity has lost its direction

After obtaining v², choose the sign using the initial velocity and the current segment of motion. Use the square root only where v²≥0. A zero can describe a genuine turning point, an asymptotically approached point, or the end of the stated force law. Test rather than guessing.

Time comes from one more separation

\[\begin{gathered}t-t_0=\int_{x_0}^{x}\frac{ds}{v(s)}\end{gathered}\]

If the integral diverges as x approaches a candidate endpoint, that point is not reached at finite time. A simple zero of v with v proportional to the remaining distance produces a logarithmic divergence. Conversely, a formula growing without bound at finite time must be restricted before that singular time.

An inverse-square attraction has an escape threshold

For acceleration −k/x², launched outwards from x=a with speed u,

\[\begin{gathered}v^2=u^2+2k\left(\frac1x-\frac1a\right)\end{gathered}\]

A finite upper turning position exists when u²<2k/a. At equality the particle can travel arbitrarily far while its speed tends to zero; above equality it has a positive limiting outward speed. The initial direction and the x>0 domain remain part of this statement.

Velocity-dependent laws can also simplify in position

If acceleration has a factor v, the equation v dv/dx may cancel that factor on a nonzero-velocity branch. Check the lost v=0 case separately. For a constant-power drive opposed by quadratic resistance, working with v³ as a function of x is often simpler than integrating with respect to time.

Verify the proposed function

Check v dv/dx against the original signed acceleration, the initial speed and position, and the allowed coordinate interval. If a time formula is available, also check dx/dt=v(x(t)). These checks catch a missing factor of two and an incorrect square-root sign.
lessons.method:
1. Choose the signed coordinate and one physically consistent branch.
  2. Replace acceleration by v dv/dx and separate or integrate.
  3. Apply the initial velocity condition to v², then select the sign of v.
  4. Integrate dx/v if time or reachability is required.
  5. Check every domain boundary and differentiate back into the force law.
mistakes: The integral of acceleration with respect to x gives v²/2, not v.
A square root does not choose the velocity direction for you.
A zero of v² need not be reached in finite time.
Do not divide by v without considering any lost rest solution.
Continue a branch only up to its first valid boundary.

examples.title: 1 · Integrate v dv, not just dv
examples.question: A particle starts at x=0 with speed 8 m s⁻¹. For x≥0 its acceleration is \(-12x^2\) m s⁻². Find its forward velocity and first turning position.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v\frac{dv}{dx}=-12x^2\\\frac12(v^2-64)=-4x^3\\v=\sqrt{64-8x^3}\\0\le x\le2,\qquad x_{\rm turn}=2\end{gathered}\]

The positive square root describes the outward segment. At the turn acceleration is −48 m s⁻², so a negative-velocity return segment follows if the force law continues to hold.

examples.title: 2 · Find a finite upper turning position
examples.question: A particle moves outwards from x=2 m with speed 4 m s⁻¹ under acceleration \(-20/x^2\) m s⁻². Find v² and the greatest distance from the origin.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\frac12(v^2-16)=\int_2^x-\frac{20}{s^2}\,ds\\v^2=\frac{40}{x}-4\\x_{\max}=10\end{gathered}\]

The outward branch has v>0 for 2≤x<10. This is below the escape threshold because the initial speed squared 16 is below 2k/a=20.

examples.title: 3 · A zero velocity reached only in a limit
examples.question: A particle initially at x=1 m has forward velocity \(v=4(3-x)\) m s⁻¹ on x<3. Find its acceleration as a function of x and its trajectory. Can it reach x=3 at finite time?
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}a=v\frac{dv}{dx}=16(x-3)\\\frac{dx}{3-x}=4\,dt\\x=3-2e^{-4t}\\x\lt3\quad\text{for every finite }t\ge0\end{gathered}\]

Velocity stays positive and tends to zero. The time integral diverges logarithmically as x approaches 3; the zero in the velocity formula is not a finite-time reversal.

examples.title: 4 · An outward model with a finite-time pole
examples.question: A particle starts at x=0 with velocity 4 m s⁻¹ and has acceleration \(2x^3+8x\) m s⁻² on x≥0. Find x(t) and the maximal non-negative finite branch beginning at t=0.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v^2=16+x^4+8x^2=(x^2+4)^2\\v=x^2+4\\\int_0^x\frac{ds}{s^2+4}=t\\\frac12\tan^{-1}\left(\frac x2\right)=t\\x=2\tan(2t)\\0\le t\lt\frac\pi4\end{gathered}\]

The coordinate grows without bound at π/4 in this ideal model. The tangent formula beyond its first pole is not a continuation of the specified forward trajectory.

lessons.title: Resistance, first stops and changes of direction
lessons.summary: Separate the velocity equation and keep drag opposite to the actual motion.
lessons.objective: Solve resistance models on valid ascent, descent and stopping branches without inventing a restart.
lessons.before: Complete time-dependent motion and the v dv/dx link. Review logarithmic integration and the substitution v=b tanθ for a quadratic denominator. All forces must be resolved along the chosen positive axis.
lessons.ideas:
Speed and signed velocity play different roles

A resistance opposes the instantaneous motion. If signed velocity is w, linear drag has signed force −cw, and quadratic drag has signed force −kw|w|. A specified force that always points in one fixed direction is a different model. Its sign need not reverse with the motion.

Separate a velocity-only equation

\[\begin{gathered}\frac{dv}{dt}=f(v)\\t-t_0=\int_{v_0}^{v}\frac{ds}{f(s)}\end{gathered}\]

Keep the constant-velocity solutions f(v)=0 that division would remove. With positive forward speed and deceleration −(A+Bv), integrate 1/(A+Bv). Stop using the forward formula at its first zero unless the next force model has been justified.

A square can hide a branch restriction

For resistance proportional to √v, separation first gives an expression for the non-negative quantity √v. That expression cannot be continued after it becomes negative and then squared to produce a supposed restart. If no drive acts and the force is zero at rest, the later solution remains v=0.

Ascent and descent require separate force equations

For upward speed v during ascent with quadratic resistance, gravity and resistance both act downwards. Using a downward speed s during descent reverses the direction of resistance relative to the coordinate:

\[\begin{gathered}\frac{dv}{dt}=-g-kv^2\quad\text{(ascent)}\\\frac{ds}{dt}=g-ks^2\quad\text{(descent)}\end{gathered}\]

Use the top state as the descent initial condition. The return speed is smaller than launch speed because resistance does negative work on both legs. Conservation of mechanical energy over the whole journey is therefore invalid.

A quadratic denominator stays within ordinary calculus

\[\begin{gathered}\int\frac{dv}{b^2+v^2}=\frac1b\tan^{-1}\left(\frac vb\right)+C\end{gathered}\]

This follows from v=b tanθ. For b²−v² use partial fractions and logarithms on the relevant branch. Inverse hyperbolic functions and an integrating factor are not required here.

Test the first event

Choose the first positive stopping or turning time, check that the stated position can be reached before it, and use speed |w| rather than a signed component when giving a speed. For friction, its law at permanent rest may differ from its sliding value.
lessons.method:
1. Choose a positive direction and write the signed weight, drag and other forces.
  2. Separate the equation and apply the initial speed.
  3. Keep root/logarithm sign restrictions and any lost constant solution.
  4. Find the first zero or switch and form the next branch separately.
  5. Check force direction, event order and the actual distance or speed requested.
mistakes: A resistance always opposes motion; a fixed-direction force need not.
A squared formula does not justify a negative square-root branch.
Do not extend a forward-speed formula through a first stop automatically.
Gravity and resistance have different relative signs on ascent and descent.
Do not conserve mechanical energy through a resistive round trip.

examples.title: 1 · Stop at the first zero of the forward solution
examples.question: A trolley starts at O with speed 10 m s⁻¹ and obeys \(dv/dt=-(v+2)/3\) while moving forwards. There is no drive and it remains at rest after its first stop. Find the stopping time and distance.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\frac{dv}{v+2}=-\frac13\,dt\\v=12e^{-t/3}-2\\T=3\ln6\\x=36(1-e^{-t/3})-2t\\s=30-6\ln6\end{gathered}\]

The formula is used only for 0≤t≤T. A later negative algebraic value would not describe a new forward speed under the stated post-stop model.

examples.title: 2 · The unsquared expression must stay non-negative
examples.question: A particle starts at speed 9 m s⁻¹ with \(dv/dt=-3\sqrt v\) while moving. At rest the force is zero and there is no drive. Find its first stopping time, distance before stopping and later speed.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}2\sqrt v=6-3t\\v=\left(3-\frac32t\right)^2\quad(0\le t\le2)\\T=2,\qquad s=\int_0^2v\,dt=6\\v=0\quad(t\ge2)\end{gathered}\]

After t=2, the expression 3−3t/2 is negative. Squaring it would invent a restart and would no longer satisfy the original resistance equation.

examples.title: 3 · Upward motion under linear air resistance
examples.question: A particle is projected vertically upwards at 25 m s⁻¹. During ascent it obeys \(dv/dt=-10-v/5\), with upward positive and x=0 at launch. Find its trajectory and greatest height.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v=75e^{-t/5}-50\\T=5\ln\left(\frac32\right)\\x=375(1-e^{-t/5})-50t\\H=125-250\ln\left(\frac32\right)\end{gathered}\]

These ascent expressions end at v=0. For descent the signed-velocity convention must still keep resistance opposite to the motion.

examples.title: 4 · Derive a separate descent law
examples.question: A particle is launched upwards at \(\sqrt{3g/k}\). Weight and quadratic resistance \(mk s^2\), opposing motion at speed s, act throughout. Find the maximum height and return speed to launch level.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v\frac{dv}{dx}=-g-kv^2\\g+kv^2=4g\,e^{-2kx}\\H=\frac{\ln4}{2k}=\frac{\ln2}{k}\\s\frac{ds}{dy}=g-ks^2\\s^2=\frac gk(1-e^{-2ky})\\s_{\rm return}=\sqrt{\frac{3g}{4k}}\end{gathered}\]

Here y is distance downwards from the top. At return y=H. The return speed is half the launch speed, consistently with energy dissipated on both legs.

lessons.title: Limiting speeds, finite travel and constant power
lessons.summary: Use the force balance as a candidate limit, then prove reachability from the trajectory.
lessons.objective: Distinguish asymptotic limits from finite events and solve constant-power motion using the appropriate variable.
lessons.before: Complete resistance branches and position–velocity links. Review exponential limits, logarithmic integrals and power as force times velocity. The constant-power driving law used below is specified for positive speed.
lessons.ideas:
Zero acceleration identifies a candidate limiting speed

For v′=A−cv with A,c positive, the equilibrium speed is L=A/c. Separation gives

\[\begin{gathered}v=L+(u-L)e^{-ct}\\x=x_0+Lt+\frac{u-L}{c}(1-e^{-ct})\end{gathered}\]

If u<L the speed increases; if u>L it decreases. Unless u=L initially, the exponential difference is nonzero at every finite time. The balance A−cL=0 alone does not prove that the trajectory tends to L or reaches it.

Quadratic drag has two non-equilibrium branches

For v′=k(L²−v²), partial fractions give a logarithm involving (v−L)/(v+L). Below L and above L have different initial signs; keep the correct branch and exclude v=L only after recording it as a constant solution. An exponential form avoids needing inverse hyperbolic notation.

Zero limiting speed does not decide total distance

A positive speed proportional to (1+t)⁻² has a convergent displacement integral. A speed proportional to (1+t)⁻¹ or (1+t)⁻¹/² has an unbounded integral. Check ∫v dt or x(t), not merely the limit of v. Also distinguish a finite limiting position from a finite-time stopping position.

Constant power is not constant force

\[\begin{gathered}\mathcal P=F_{\rm drive}v\\F_{\rm drive}=\frac{\mathcal P}{v}\end{gathered}\]

For a particle of mass m, write the driving power as mP and quadratic resistance as mkv². On v>0,

\[\begin{gathered}v\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac Pv-kv^2\\w=v^3,\qquad\frac{dw}{dx}=3(P-kw)\\w=\frac Pk+\left(u^3-\frac Pk\right)e^{-3k(x-x_0)}\end{gathered}\]

This follows by separation in w. The limiting speed is the cube root of P/k, and the actual driving power is mP. Do not set P equal to a force. After a switch, x₀ and u refer to the switch state, not the original launch.

A requested target may not be reachable

If a target speed lies strictly below an approached upper limit, the logarithmic event expression can give a finite time or distance. Equality is a limiting event; a larger target is not reached on that branch. Check positivity of every logarithm argument and the direction of change before accepting a formula.
lessons.method:
1. Find constant-speed candidates from the signed force balance.
  2. Solve with the actual initial speed and select the correct branch.
  3. Check limits, monotonicity and finite-time denominators.
  4. For a constant-power drive consider w=v³ as a function of position.
  5. Test strict target reachability and distinguish time, distance and limiting position.
mistakes: A zero acceleration equation is not itself proof of finite-time attainment.
An initial speed above a terminal value must decrease towards it.
A speed tending to zero can still produce unbounded total distance.
Constant driving power gives a force inversely proportional to speed.
At a switch, use the switch position and velocity as the new initial state.

examples.title: 1 · Reach a lower target before the limit
examples.question: A particle starts at x=0 with speed 2 m s⁻¹ and obeys \(dv/dt=18-3v\). Find the time and displacement at speed 5 m s⁻¹, and state its limiting speed.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v=6-4e^{-3t}\\x=6t-\frac43(1-e^{-3t})\\v=5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T=\frac{\ln4}{3}\\x(T)=2\ln4-1\\v\longrightarrow6\end{gathered}\]

The target 5 is attained at finite time. The limit 6 is not, because the exponential term never vanishes at finite time.

examples.title: 2 · A quadratic-drag model from rest
examples.question: A particle starts from rest at x=0 with \(dv/dt=16-v^2\). Find v(t), then the time and distance needed to reach half its limiting speed. Use exponentials.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v=4\frac{e^{8t}-1}{e^{8t}+1}\\v=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T=\frac{\ln3}{8}\\v\frac{dv}{dx}=16-v^2\\v^2=16(1-e^{-2x})\\x=\frac12\ln\left(\frac43\right)\end{gathered}\]

The limiting speed is 4 m s⁻¹. The selected branch rises from zero and stays below 4 at every finite time.

examples.title: 3 · Slowing forever without finite total travel
examples.question: A particle starts at O with speed 3 m s⁻¹ and has \(dv/dt=-v^3/6\). Find its speed and displacement, and decide whether total distance is finite.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\frac1{v^2}=\frac19+\frac t3\\v=\frac3{\sqrt{1+3t}}\\x=2(\sqrt{1+3t}-1)\end{gathered}\]

The speed is positive for every finite t and tends to zero, but x grows without bound. This contrasts with the finite-distance example in the time-dependent lesson.

examples.title: 4 · Change variable to the cube of speed
examples.question: A 1 kg particle moves forwards under a constant-power drive of 16 W and resistance \(v^2/4\) N. Initially x=0 and v=2 m s⁻¹. Find v³ as a function of x, the limiting speed and the distance to reach v=3.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v^2\frac{dv}{dx}=16-\frac14v^3\\w=v^3,\qquad\frac{dw}{dx}=48-\frac34w\\v^3=64-56e^{-3x/4}\\v_{\rm limit}=4\\x=\frac43\ln\left(\frac{56}{37}\right)\end{gathered}\]

The target 3 lies between the initial speed and the limit, so it is reached at finite positive distance. The driving force is 16/v N, not 16 N.

The particle first turns when \(v=0\), at \(t=2\pi/3\). For return to \(O\), \[2\cos\left(\frac\pi3-\frac T2\right)=1.\] After the turning time the relevant angle is \(-\pi/3\), not \(+\pi/3\), which corresponds to launch. Therefore \(T=4\pi/3\). questions.title: Upward projection with linear air resistance
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is projected vertically upwards from \(O\) at \(18\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It experiences gravity and air resistance of magnitude \(mv/2\) N, where \(v\) is its speed. During ascent let \(x\) be its height above \(O\) and let \(v\gt 0\) be its upward velocity. Use \(g=10\).

  1. Find \(v(t)\) during ascent.

    [4]

  2. Find \(x(t)\) during ascent.

    [3]

  3. Find the greatest height reached, giving an exact expression and a value to three significant figures.

    [3]

(a)

\(v=38e^{-t/2}-20\).

(b)

\(x=76(1-e^{-t/2})-20t\).

(c)

Both gravity and resistance act downwards during ascent. Hence \[m\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=-10m-\frac12mv, \qquad \frac{\mathrm dv}{v+20}=-\frac12\,\mathrm dt.\] Integrating and applying \(v(0)=18\), \[\ln\frac{v+20}{38}=-\frac t2.\] Thus \(v=38e^{-t/2}-20\), until this upward velocity first becomes zero.

Part (b)

Integrate the upward velocity from launch: \[x=\int_0^t(38e^{-q/2}-20)\,\mathrm dq =76(1-e^{-t/2})-20t.\] This satisfies \(x(0)=0\), and its derivative agrees with the velocity in part (a).

Part (c)

At the highest point, \(38e^{-T/2}=20\). Thus \[T=2\ln\frac{19}{10}.\] Substitution gives \[H=76\left(1-\frac{10}{19}\right)-40\ln\frac{19}{10} =36-40\ln\frac{19}{10}=10.3258\ldots.\] The upward speed is positive before this time and zero here, so this is the first maximum. Afterward, resistance acts upwards. If downward speed is denoted by \(w\gt 0\), its equation is \(w'=10-w/2\), not \(w'=-10-w/2\).

questions.title: Quadratic air resistance during ascent
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is projected vertically upwards from \(O\) at \(15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Air resistance has magnitude \(2mv^2/45\) N and opposes the motion. During ascent, \(x\) metres is the height above \(O\) and \(v\gt 0\) is the upward speed. Use \(g=10\). You may use the substitution \(v=15\tan\phi\).

  1. Find \(v\) as a function of \(x\) during ascent, stating the height interval on which this branch is valid.

    [5]

  2. Find \(v\) as a function of \(t\) during ascent and state the time at which the highest point is reached.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v=15\sqrt{2e^{-4x/45}-1}\), \(0\leq x\leq(45/4)\ln2\).

(b)

\(v=15\tan(\pi/4-2t/3)\), \(0\leq t\leq3\pi/8\); highest point at \(3\pi/8\,\mathrm s\).

Part (a)

During ascent both forces act downwards. Therefore \[v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=-10-\frac2{45}v^2 =-\frac2{45}(v^2+225).\] Separate and integrate: \[\int\frac{v\,\mathrm dv}{v^2+225}=-\frac2{45}\int\mathrm dx, \qquad \frac12\ln(v^2+225)=-\frac2{45}x+C.\] At \(x=0,v=15\), \(v^2+225=450\). Hence \[v^2+225=450e^{-4x/45}.\] The upward branch is \[v=15\sqrt{2e^{-4x/45}-1}.\] It is real and nonnegative on \(0\leq x\leq(45/4)\ln2\), with the upper endpoint the maximum height. The negative square root is not the ascent speed.

Part (b)

Using acceleration as \(\mathrm dv/\mathrm dt\), \[\int\frac{\mathrm dv}{v^2+225}=-\frac2{45}t+C.\] With \(v=15\tan\phi\), the left side is \(\phi/15\). The initial condition is \(\phi(0)=\pi/4\), giving \[\phi=\frac\pi4-\frac23t,\qquad v=15\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\frac23t\right).\] The first zero is reached at \(t=3\pi/8\). This is the endpoint of ascent; after it, a positive downward speed requires a different force equation because the air resistance reverses.

questions.title: The return speed is not the launch speed
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is projected vertically upwards from \(O\) with speed \(2\sqrt{g/k}\), where \(k\gt 0\). The air resistance has magnitude \(mks^2\), where \(s\) is the instantaneous speed, and always opposes motion. No other force except weight acts. The particle eventually returns to \(O\).

  1. Find the maximum height \(H\) above \(O\).

    [3]

  2. Form a separate equation for descent and find the speed on return to \(O\). Explain why mechanical energy cannot be conserved over the complete journey.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(H=\ln5/(2k)\).

(b)

\(s_{\mathrm{return}}=\sqrt{4g/(5k)}\). Resistance does negative work on both ascent and descent.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

During ascent, let \(v\gt 0\) be upward speed and \(x\) height. Then \[v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=-g-kv^2.\] Separate and integrate from \(v=2\sqrt{g/k},x=0\) to \(v=0,x=H\): \[H=\int_0^{2\sqrt{g/k}}\frac{v}{g+kv^2}\,\mathrm dv =\frac1{2k}\ln\frac{g+4g}{g} =\frac{\ln5}{2k}.\]

Part (b)

Measure \(z\) downwards from the highest point and let \(w\gt 0\) be downward speed. Resistance now acts upwards, giving \[w\frac{\mathrm dw}{\mathrm dz}=g-kw^2.\] Starting from \(w=0\) at \(z=0\), integration gives \[-\frac1{2k}\ln\frac{g-kw^2}{g}=z, \qquad w^2=\frac gk(1-e^{-2kz}).\] At return, \(z=H\), so \(e^{-2kH}=1/5\) and \[w^2=\frac{4g}{5k},\qquad w=\sqrt{\frac{4g}{5k}}.\] The return speed is smaller than the launch speed. The change of direction reverses the resistance, not its dissipative effect: it does negative work throughout both moving stages. Gravity alone is conservative, so gravitational potential plus kinetic energy is not conserved here.
questions.hint_html: Use a new downward displacement measured from the highest point. The drag term changes sign in the equation for positive downward speed.

questions.title: A trolley slowed by two different resistances
questions.prompt_html:
A trolley, modelled as a particle of mass \(m\), is launched at speed \(U\) along a rough horizontal track. While its forward speed is \(v\gt 0\), it experiences a drag force of magnitude \(mgkv\) and sliding friction of magnitude \(\mu mg\), both opposing motion. Here \(k\gt 0\) and \(\mu\gt 0\). There is no driving force.

  1. By forming and solving a differential equation, express \(v\) in terms of \(t\).

    [4]

  2. For \(U=12\), \(k=0.05\), \(\mu=0.15\) and \(g=10\), find the stopping time and stopping distance in exact form.

    [4]

  3. Find the average speed while the trolley is moving, to three significant figures.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v=(U+\mu/k)e^{-gkt}-\mu/k\), up to the first stop.

(b)

\(T=2\ln5\,\mathrm s\); \(s=24-6\ln5\,\mathrm m\).

(c)

\(12/\ln5-3=4.46\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Choose the initial direction as positive. Newton's second law gives \[m\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=-mgkv-\mu mg.\] Thus \(\mathrm dv/(kv+\mu)=-g\,\mathrm dt\). Integrating and using \(v(0)=U\), \[\frac1k\ln\frac{kv+\mu}{kU+\mu}=-gt.\] Consequently \[v=\left(U+\frac\mu k\right)e^{-gkt}-\frac\mu k.\] The formula applies while the trolley is moving forwards. Once it stops, neither the friction model nor the meaning of forward speed permits extending this formula to negative values.

Part (b)

Here \(v=15e^{-t/2}-3\). Setting \(v=0\) gives \(e^{-T/2}=1/5\), so \(T=2\ln5\).

The displacement while moving is \[x(t)=\int_0^t(15e^{-q/2}-3)\,\mathrm dq=30(1-e^{-t/2})-3t.\] It increases until \(T\); hence the stopping distance is \[s=30\left(1-\frac15\right)-6\ln5=24-6\ln5.\] This is approximately \(14.343\,\mathrm m\). After this instant the trolley remains at rest.

Part (c)

Average speed is distance divided by elapsed time, not the average of the endpoint speeds: \[\overline v=\frac{24-6\ln5}{2\ln5}=\frac{12}{\ln5}-3=4.456\ldots.\] Therefore the average speed is \(4.46\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
questions.hint_html: Use the signed force equation only until \(v=0\); integrate the resulting velocity over that interval.

questions.title: Why squaring an expression can invent a restart
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves along a horizontal line with initial speed \(16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). While it is moving, the only horizontal force is a resistance of magnitude \[\frac{24\sqrt v}{(1+t)^2}\ \mathrm N,\] where \(v\geq0\) is speed and \(t\geq0\) is time. At rest the horizontal force is zero.

  1. Find \(v(t)\) up to the first stopping instant.

    [4]

  2. State the first stopping time and the speed for later times.

    [1]

(a)

\(v=[6/(1+t)-2]^2=4(2-t)^2/(1+t)^2\) for \(0\leq t\leq2\).

(b)

First stop: \(t=2\,\mathrm s\). For \(t\geq2\), \(v=0\).

Newton's law gives \[\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=-\frac{12\sqrt v}{(1+t)^2}.\] For \(v\gt 0\), separate and integrate: \[2\sqrt v=\frac{12}{1+t}+C.\] Since \(v(0)=16\), \(C=-4\). Hence \[\sqrt v=\frac6{1+t}-2.\] The left side cannot be negative, so this relation applies only for \(t\leq2\). Squaring on this valid interval gives the required formula, extended continuously to the stopping endpoint.

Part (b)

The first zero is at \(6/(1+t)-2=0\), so \(t=2\). The particle subsequently remains at rest: there is no driving force. Continuing the squared expression for \(t\gt 2\) would predict increasing speed and would not satisfy the original resistive equation.

questions.title: Finding a resistance law from stopping measurements
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) moves on a horizontal line against a resistance of magnitude \(mk\sqrt v\) N, where \(k\gt 0\) and \(v\) is its speed. Its initial speed is \(u\gt 0\). It first comes to rest after \(4\) seconds, having travelled \(12\) metres. No driving force acts.

  1. Find \(v(t)\) before the first stop in terms of \(u\) and \(k\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(u\) and \(k\).

    [4]

  3. Find the first time at which the speed is half its initial value.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v=(\sqrt u-kt/2)^2\), \(0\leq t\leq2\sqrt u/k\).

(b)

\(u=9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), \(k=3/2\) in the stated SI model.

(c)

\(t=4-2\sqrt2\,\mathrm s\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Newton's law is \(v'=-k\sqrt v\). For \(v\gt 0\), separation gives \[2\sqrt v=-kt+C.\] The initial condition gives \(C=2\sqrt u\). Thus \[\sqrt v=\sqrt u-\frac k2t,\qquad v=\left(\sqrt u-\frac k2t\right)^2.\] The root on the first line is nonnegative only up to \(T=2\sqrt u/k\), the first stopping time.

Part (b)

Since the stopping time is \(T=4\), \(k=\sqrt u/2\). Substituting this in part (a), \[v=u\left(1-\frac t4\right)^2,\qquad0\leq t\leq4.\] The distance is \[12=\int_0^4u(1-t/4)^2\,\mathrm dt=\frac{4u}{3}.\] Therefore \(u=9\), and \(k=\sqrt9/2=3/2\). Both constants are positive as required.

Part (c)

For \(0\leq t\leq4\), the factor \(1-t/4\) is nonnegative. Thus \[\left(1-\frac t4\right)^2=\frac12 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 1-\frac t4=\frac1{\sqrt2}.\] Hence \(t=4-2\sqrt2\). The root with a plus sign would lie beyond the first stop and would be an artefact of continuing the squared formula.

questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is launched along a horizontal line at an unknown speed \(u\gt 0\). It experiences only resistance of magnitude \(mkv^2\) N, where \(k\gt 0\). Its speed is \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) after \(2\) seconds and \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) after \(6\) seconds.

  2. Find the distance travelled when the speed is first one quarter of the initial speed.

    [3]

(a)

\(u=12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), \(k=1/24\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}\).

(b)

\(24\ln4\,\mathrm m\).

(c)

No: \(v=24/(t+2)\gt 0\) for every finite \(t\geq0\).

Part (a)

Newton's law gives \(v'=-kv^2\). Separating and integrating with \(v(0)=u\), \[\frac1v=kt+\frac1u.\] The measurements imply \[\frac16=2k+\frac1u,\qquad \frac13=6k+\frac1u.\] Subtracting, \(1/6=4k\), so \(k=1/24\). Then \(1/u=1/6-1/12=1/12\), and \(u=12\).

The calibrated velocity is \[v=\frac{24}{t+2}.\] Hence the displacement from launch is \[x(t)=24\ln\frac{t+2}{2}.\] One quarter of the initial speed is 3, already known to occur at \(t=6\). Thus \(x=24\ln4\).

The denominator \(t+2\) is finite and positive for every finite nonnegative time, so the speed cannot be zero. It only tends to zero as \(t\to\infty\).

questions.title: Cubic drag: slowing without a final stopping point
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) starts at \(O\) with speed \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) along a horizontal line. The only horizontal force is a resistance of magnitude \(mv^3/8\) N, where \(v\) is the positive speed in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

(a)

\(v=4/\sqrt{1+4t}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

(b)

\(6\,\mathrm m\); the total distance is unbounded although \(v\to0\).

Newton's law gives \(\mathrm dv/\mathrm dt=-v^3/8\). With \(v=2\) at \(t=0\), \[\frac{6+v}{6-v}=2e^{12t}.\] Solving for \(v\) gives \[v=6\frac{2e^{12t}-1}{2e^{12t}+1}.\]

Part (b)

At \(v=5\), \[\frac{6+5}{6-5}=2e^{12t},\qquad t=\frac1{12}\ln\frac{11}{2}.\] Dividing numerator and denominator of \(v(t)\) by \(e^{12t}\) shows that \(v\to6\). Also \(v=6-12/(2e^{12t}+1)\lt 6\), so this limiting speed is never attained in finite time.

questions.title: Reaching a prescribed fraction of the limiting speed
questions.prompt_html:
A particle moves on a horizontal line with initial velocity \(u\gt 0\) and initial displacement zero. Its signed acceleration is \(k(4u-v)\), where \(k\gt 0\) is constant and \(v\) is its velocity.

  1. Find the first time at which its velocity is \(3u\).

    [4]

  2. Find the displacement at this time. Explain why the speed has not reached its limiting value.

    [4]

(a)

\(T=\ln3/k\).

(b)

\(s=(u/k)(4\ln3-2)\); the limiting speed is \(4u\gt 3u\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The differential equation is \[\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=k(4u-v).\] Separate and integrate with \(v(0)=u\): \[-\ln\frac{4u-v}{3u}=kt,\qquad v=4u-3ue^{-kt}.\] At \(v=3u\), \(e^{-kT}=1/3\), so \(T=\ln3/k\). Since \(v'=3ku e^{-kt}\gt 0\), this time is unique.

Part (b)

Integrating the velocity from zero gives \[x=4ut-\frac{3u}{k}(1-e^{-kt}).\] At \(T=\ln3/k\), \[s=\frac{4u}{k}\ln3-\frac{3u}{k}(1-1/3) =\frac uk(4\ln3-2).\] For every finite time, \(3ue^{-kt}\gt 0\), so \(v\lt 4u\). The limiting speed \(4u\) is approached asymptotically; the attained speed \(3u\) is strictly smaller.

questions.title: Linear resistance on a smooth inclined plane
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is released from rest on a smooth plane inclined at angle \(\alpha\), where \(\sin\alpha=3/5\). A resistance of magnitude \(mkv\) N acts up the plane when the particle moves down it at speed \(v\), where \(k\gt 0\).

    [5]

  2. State the limiting speed.

    [1]

(a)

\(v=\frac{3g}{5k}(1-e^{-kt})\).

(b)

\(3g/(5k)\).

Part (a)

Resolve parallel to the plane, positive down its line of greatest slope: \[m\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=mg\sin\alpha-mkv =m\left(\frac35g-kv\right).\] The normal reaction balances the perpendicular component of weight and does not enter this equation. Separate and integrate: \[\frac{\mathrm dv}{3g/5-kv}=\mathrm dt, \qquad -\frac1k\ln\left(\frac{3g/5-kv}{3g/5}\right)=t.\] Here the initial condition \(v=0\) has fixed the constant. Rearranging, \[v=\frac{3g}{5k}(1-e^{-kt}).\]

Part (b)

As \(t\to\infty\), \(e^{-kt}\to0\), so the speed approaches \(3g/(5k)\). This is also the speed at which resistance balances the component of weight down the plane.

questions.title: Falling from rest with quadratic resistance
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) is released from rest at \(O\) and falls vertically. Its upward resistance is \(mv^2/90\) N, where \(v\geq0\) is downward speed. Let \(x\) be downward displacement from \(O\), and use \(g=10\).

  1. Find \(v(t)\), expressing your answer using exponentials.

    [4]

  2. Find \(v^2\) in terms of \(x\).

    [4]

  3. Find the time and distance needed to reach half the limiting speed.

    [3]

(a)

\(v=30(e^{2t/3}-1)/(e^{2t/3}+1)\).

(b)

\(v^2=900(1-e^{-x/45})\).

(c)

\(t=(3/2)\ln3\,\mathrm s\); \(x=45\ln(4/3)\,\mathrm m\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The equation is \[\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=10-\frac{v^2}{90}=\frac{900-v^2}{90}.\] Partial fractions give \[\frac1{60}\ln\frac{30+v}{30-v}=\frac t{90}+C.\] At release \(v=0\), so \(C=0\). Thus \[\frac{30+v}{30-v}=e^{2t/3},\qquad v=30\frac{e^{2t/3}-1}{e^{2t/3}+1}.\] This solution satisfies \(0\leq v\lt 30\), as required for the chosen logarithmic branch.

Part (b)

Use \(a=v\,\mathrm dv/\mathrm dx\): \[v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{900-v^2}{90}.\] Hence \[\int\frac{v}{900-v^2}\,\mathrm dv=\int\frac1{90}\,\mathrm dx, \qquad -\frac12\ln(900-v^2)=\frac x{90}+C.\] With \(v=0,x=0\), this becomes \[\ln\frac{900-v^2}{900}=-\frac x{45},\] which gives \(v^2=900(1-e^{-x/45})\). The formula extends continuously to the release point even though the subsequent motion has \(v\gt 0\).

Part (c)

The limiting speed is 30, so the target is 15. Part (a) gives \[e^{2t/3}=\frac{30+15}{30-15}=3, \qquad t=\frac32\ln3.\] From part (b), \[225=900(1-e^{-x/45}),\qquad e^{-x/45}=\frac34.\] Thus \(x=45\ln(4/3)\). Both values are finite because the target is strictly below the limiting speed.

questions.title: Recovering a force from a displacement–velocity relation
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves on a horizontal line. Its displacement \(x\) metres from \(O\) and signed velocity \(v\) satisfy \[\frac vx=\frac{4-2t}{1+t},\qquad t\geq0.\] Initially \(x=2\). The resultant horizontal force is \(F\), positive in the direction of increasing \(x\).

  1. Find \(x\) as a function of \(t\).

    [4]

  2. Find the magnitude and direction of \(F\) at the first instant when the particle is at rest.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(x=2(1+t)^6e^{-2t}\).

(b)

\(2916e^{-4}\,\mathrm N\), towards \(O\), at \(t=2\,\mathrm s\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Use \(v=x'\) and write \[\frac1x\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=\frac6{1+t}-2.\] Integrating gives \(\ln x=6\ln(1+t)-2t+C\) on the positive branch selected by \(x(0)=2\). Thus \(C=\ln2\) and \[x=2(1+t)^6e^{-2t}.\] This remains positive for all \(t\geq0\), so division by \(x\) has not excluded a point of the resulting trajectory.

Part (b)

Since \(x\gt 0\), the first zero of \(v=x(4-2t)/(1+t)\) is \(t=2\). Put \(f(t)=(4-2t)/(1+t)\). Then \[x''=x(f^2+f'),\qquad f'=-\frac6{(1+t)^2}.\] At \(t=2\), \(f=0\), \(f'=-2/3\), and \(x=2\cdot3^6e^{-4}=1458e^{-4}\). Hence \[F=3x''=3(1458e^{-4})(-2/3)=-2916e^{-4}\,\mathrm N.\] The magnitude is \(2916e^{-4}\) N and the direction is towards \(O\). Zero velocity does not mean zero acceleration.

A particle of mass \(m\) moves along the positive \(x\)-axis. At time \(t\geq0\), the only horizontal force acts in the negative \(x\)-direction and has magnitude \[\frac m6(v-2)^2e^{-t}\ \mathrm N.\] At \(t=0\), \(x=2\) m and \(v=8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

\(v=2+6/(2-e^{-t})\).

\(x=2+2t+3\ln(2e^t-1)\).

questions.title: Two speed readings determine a time-dependent force
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) moves forwards on a horizontal line. Its only horizontal force is directed backwards and has magnitude \(mAe^{-bt}\) N, where \(A,b\gt 0\). Its initial speed is \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); its speeds at \(t=1\) and \(t=2\) seconds are \(8\) and \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), respectively.

  1. Find \(A\) and \(b\).

    [4]

  2. Find the distance travelled in the first two seconds.

    [3]

(a)

\(b=\ln2\), \(A=8\ln2\), in the stated SI model.

(b)

\(8+6/\ln2\,\mathrm m\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The equation is \(v'=-Ae^{-bt}\). Integration with the initial speed gives \[v=12-\frac Ab(1-e^{-bt}).\] Put \(q=e^{-b}\), so \(0\lt q\lt 1\). The two readings give \[\frac Ab(1-q)=4,\qquad \frac Ab(1-q^2)=6.\] Division gives \(1+q=3/2\), hence \(q=1/2\), \(b=\ln2\), and \(A/b=8\). Thus \(A=8\ln2\). The dimensions are \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\) for \(b\) and \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) for \(A\).

Part (b)

With these parameters, \[v=4+8e^{-(\ln2)t}.\] This is positive. Therefore \[s=\int_0^2(4+8e^{-(\ln2)t})\,\mathrm dt =8+\frac8{\ln2}\left(1-\frac14\right) =8+\frac6{\ln2}.\] The speed approaches 4, so extrapolating a constant deceleration from the two readings would give the wrong motion.

questions.title: A force switches off after the particle reverses
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) is initially at \(O\) with velocity \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) along a horizontal line. Its resultant force in the positive direction is \[F=4(1-t)\ \mathrm N\quad(0\leq t\leq4).\] For \(t\gt 4\), the resultant horizontal force is zero. Let \(x\) be signed displacement from \(O\).

  1. Find \(v(t)\) and \(x(t)\) for \(0\leq t\leq4\).

    [3]

  2. Find the total distance travelled by \(t=4\), in exact form.

    [3]

  3. Find the time at which the particle first returns to \(O\).

    [2]

  4. Find the total work done by the resultant force during the first four seconds.

    [2]

(a)

\(v=6+2t-t^2\), \(x=6t+t^2-t^3/3\).

(b)

\((28\sqrt7-16)/3\,\mathrm m\).

(c)

\(t=40/3\,\mathrm s\).

(d)

\(-32\,\mathrm J\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Newton's law gives \(a=F/2=2-2t\). Integrating with \(v(0)=6\), \[v=6+2t-t^2.\] Integrating again with \(x(0)=0\), \[x=6t+t^2-\frac{t^3}{3}.\] Both expressions apply only up to the force-switching time.

Part (b)

Velocity first vanishes when \(t^2-2t-6=0\), so \[t_R=1+\sqrt7\lt 4.\] It is positive before this time and negative afterward. Substitution gives \[x_R=\frac{20+14\sqrt7}{3},\qquad x(4)=\frac{56}{3}.\] Thus the particle travels out to \(x_R\) and back by \(x_R-x(4)\). Its total distance is \[x_R+(x_R-x(4))=\frac{28\sqrt7-16}{3}.\] Using only \(x(4)\) would give the displacement, not the distance.

Part (c)

At \(t=4\), \(x=56/3\gt 0\) and \(v=6+8-16=-2\). After the force switches off this velocity remains constant, rather than becoming zero. The remaining travel time is \((56/3)/2=28/3\). Therefore the first return is at \(4+28/3=40/3\) s. There was no earlier return because \(x\gt 0\) throughout \(0\lt t\leq4\).

Part (d)

The work–energy relation uses the endpoint velocities even when the direction changes: \[W=\frac12(2)(-2)^2-\frac12(2)(6)^2=4-36=-32\,\mathrm J.\] This is net work, not the integral of the force magnitude over the total distance.

questions.title: An outward launch against an inverse-square attraction
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) moves on the positive \(x\)-axis under a force directed towards the origin, of magnitude \(mk/x^2\) N. The constant \(k\) is positive. Initially \(x=a\gt 0\) and the particle is moving away from the origin with speed \(u\gt 0\).

    [4]

  2. Find the condition for a finite greatest distance from the origin, and find that distance. Describe the two remaining cases.

    [4]

(a)

\(v^2=u^2+2k(1/x-1/a)\).

(b)

If \(u^2\lt 2k/a\), \(x_{\max}=2ak/(2k-au^2)\). At equality \(x\to\infty\) and \(v\to0\); above it \(v\to\sqrt{u^2-2k/a}\gt 0\).

Part (a)

The signed acceleration is \(-k/x^2\). Hence \[v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=-\frac{k}{x^2}.\] Integrating from \(x=a,v=u\) gives \[\frac12(v^2-u^2)=k\left(\frac1x-\frac1a\right).\] Therefore \[v^2=u^2+2k\left(\frac1x-\frac1a\right).\] The outward branch is the nonnegative square root, valid until its first zero if a zero occurs.

Part (b)

At a turning point, \[0=u^2-\frac{2k}{a}+\frac{2k}{x_{\max}}.\] A positive finite value exists exactly when \(2k/a-u^2\gt 0\), giving \[x_{\max}=\frac{2ak}{2k-au^2}\gt a.\] Near this point \(v^2\) has a simple zero because its derivative is \(-2k/x_{\max}^2\ne0\). The time integral behaves like \(\int\mathrm dx/\sqrt{x_{\max}-x}\), which is finite; the particle genuinely turns.

If \(u^2=2k/a\), then \(v^2=2k/x\gt 0\) for every finite \(x\), so there is no finite turning point. The particle travels arbitrarily far while its speed tends to zero.

If \(u^2\gt 2k/a\), the velocity remains positive and approaches \(\sqrt{u^2-2k/a}\). Again there is no finite greatest distance. These conclusions come from the model, not from a claim that its force law is realistic at all scales.

questions.title: Opposing spatial forces and an inaccessible rest point
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves forwards on a horizontal line. For its forward motion at position \(x\geq0\), a force \(108/(x+2)^2\) N acts forwards and a resistance \(648/(x+2)^3\) N acts backwards. Initially \(x=0\) and \(v=6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

  1. Find the forward velocity in terms of \(x\) before any rest point.

    [4]

  2. Does the particle reach \(x=4\) at a finite time? Justify your answer by integration.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v=3(4-x)/(x+2)\), for \(0\leq x\lt 4\).

(b)

No: \(t=-x/3-2\ln[(4-x)/4]\to\infty\) as \(x\to4^-\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Newton's law gives \[v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{54}{(x+2)^2}-\frac{324}{(x+2)^3}.\] Integrate and apply \(v=6\) at \(x=0\): \[v^2=-\frac{108}{x+2}+\frac{324}{(x+2)^2}+9 =\left(\frac{18}{x+2}-3\right)^2.\] Initially \(18/(x+2)-3=6\gt 0\), so the forward branch is \[v=\frac{18}{x+2}-3=\frac{3(4-x)}{x+2}.\] It is positive on \(0\leq x\lt 4\). Squaring alone would not determine this sign.

Part (b)

For the forward branch, \[\frac{\mathrm dt}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{x+2}{3(4-x)} =-\frac13+\frac2{4-x}.\] Integrating from \(x=0,t=0\), \[t=-\frac x3-2\ln\frac{4-x}{4}.\] As \(x\to4^-\), the logarithm tends to \(-\infty\), and thus \(t\to\infty\). The speed tends to zero at a limiting position; the particle does not reach or cross that point in finite time.
questions.hint_html: After obtaining a square for \(v^2\), use the initial direction. Test a proposed stopping point by integrating \(1/v\).

Apply the initial speed and factor the result.
Select the forward branch and its interval.
Use logarithmic divergence to justify the conclusion.

questions.title: A mixed velocity law with finite-time divergence
questions.prompt_html:
A particle moves on a horizontal line with signed acceleration \[a=2v\sqrt{v+4}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}},\] where \(v\) is its velocity in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Initially \(x=1\) m and \(v=12\). Consider the forward motion from this initial state.

  1. Find \(v\) in terms of \(x\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(x(t)\) and its maximal finite interval starting at \(t=0\).

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v=(x+3)^2-4=(x+1)(x+5)\), for \(x\geq1\).

(b)

\(x=(5e^{4t}-3)/(3-e^{4t})\), \(0\leq t\lt \ln3/4\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Use \(a=v\,\mathrm dv/\mathrm dx\). The forward branch has \(v\gt 0\), so division by \(v\) is valid: \[\frac{\mathrm dv}{\sqrt{v+4}}=2\,\mathrm dx.\] Integrating, \[2\sqrt{v+4}=2x+C.\] The initial data give \(8=2+C\), so \(C=6\). Therefore \[\sqrt{v+4}=x+3,\qquad v=(x+3)^2-4.\] On \(x\geq1\), both the unsquared right side and \(v\) are positive, so the rearrangement is valid.

Part (b)

The position equation is \(x'=(x+1)(x+5)\). Partial fractions give \[\frac1{(x+1)(x+5)}=\frac14\left(\frac1{x+1}-\frac1{x+5}\right).\] Integration with \(x(0)=1\) yields \[\frac14\ln\frac{x+1}{x+5}=t+\frac14\ln\frac13.\] Thus \((x+1)/(x+5)=e^{4t}/3\), and rearrangement gives \[x=\frac{5e^{4t}-3}{3-e^{4t}}.\] The denominator is positive for \(0\leq t\lt \ln3/4\). At the endpoint it tends to zero while the numerator tends to 12, so the position diverges to \(+\infty\). Values from the negative-denominator branch are not a continuation of this forward trajectory.
questions.hint_html: First use acceleration as \(v\,\mathrm dv/\mathrm dx\); then factor the resulting quadratic before finding time.

questions.title: Exponential resistance with a nonzero limiting velocity
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves along a horizontal line. Its only horizontal force is a resistance of magnitude \[(12e^{-x}+18)e^{-x}\ \mathrm N,\] where \(x\geq0\) is displacement in metres from its initial position. At \(t=0\), its forward speed is \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

  1. Find the forward speed in terms of \(x\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(x(t)\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v=3+2e^{-x}\).

(b)

\(x=\ln[(5e^{3t}-2)/3]\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Newton's law gives \[v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=-4e^{-2x}-6e^{-x}.\] Integrating, \[v^2=4e^{-2x}+12e^{-x}+C.\] At \(x=0,v=5\), \(C=25-4-12=9\). Thus \[v^2=(3+2e^{-x})^2.\] The initial forward velocity selects \(v=3+2e^{-x}\gt 0\).

Part (b)

The position equation is \[\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=3+2e^{-x}.\] Separating, \[\int\frac{e^x}{3e^x+2}\,\mathrm dx=t+C. \] The left side is \((1/3)\ln(3e^x+2)\). Using \(x=0\) when \(t=0\), \[3e^x+2=5e^{3t}.\] Hence \(x=\ln[(5e^{3t}-2)/3]\). The logarithm argument is at least 1 for \(t\geq0\). The model predicts a decreasing speed tending to 3, consistent with a resistance tending to zero as the position grows.
questions.hint_html: After the first integration, look for a perfect square. Multiply the second separated integrand by \(e^x/e^x\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Recognise the square and choose the positive root.

questions.title: Approaching an equilibrium from the right
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves on \(x\gt 2\). Its resultant force in the positive direction is \[F=27x-\frac{432}{x^3}\ \mathrm N.\] Initially \(x=6\) m and the signed velocity is \(-16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

  1. Find \(v\) in terms of \(x\) for the initial leftward motion.

    [4]

  2. Find \(x(t)\).

    [3]

  3. Describe the limiting position and decide whether the particle reverses at a finite time.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v=-3(x^2-4)/x\).

(b)

\(x=\sqrt{4+32e^{-6t}}\).

(c)

\(x\to2^+\), \(v\to0^-\); no finite-time reversal.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Newton's law gives \[v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=9x-\frac{144}{x^3}.\] Integration gives \[v^2=9x^2+\frac{144}{x^2}+C.\] At \(x=6,v=-16\), \(256=324+4+C\), so \(C=-72\). Therefore \[v^2=9\left(x-\frac4x\right)^2.\] For \(x\gt 2\), \(x-4/x\gt 0\). The initial velocity is negative, so \[v=-3\left(x-\frac4x\right)=-\frac3x(x^2-4).\]

Part (b)

From part (a), \[\frac{x}{x^2-4}\,\mathrm dx=-3\,\mathrm dt.\] Integration gives \((1/2)\ln(x^2-4)=-3t+C\). The initial condition gives \(x^2-4=32e^{-6t}\), hence \[x=\sqrt{4+32e^{-6t}}.\] The positive square root is required because \(x\gt 2\).

Part (c)

For every finite \(t\geq0\), \(32e^{-6t}\gt 0\), so \(x\gt 2\) and the velocity in part (a) is strictly negative. Therefore no finite-time reversal occurs. As \(t\to\infty\), \(x\to2\) and \(v\to0\); the force also tends to zero. A positive force here is decelerating a leftward motion, not automatically producing rightward motion.
questions.hint_html: The square root of \(v^2\) needs the initial sign. For the second integration, use \(x\,\mathrm dx/(x^2-4)\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Select the negative branch using x>2 and the initial velocity.
Use the strict finite-time inequality to rule out reversal.

questions.title: An implicit trajectory approaching a limiting point
questions.prompt_html:
A particle moves on \(x\gt 0\) with signed acceleration \[a=\frac{288}{x^2}-\frac{576}{x^3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.\] Initially \(x=4\) m and it moves towards the origin at \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

  1. Find the signed velocity as a function of \(x\) on the initial branch.

    [4]

  2. Show that, for this trajectory, \(e^{-6t}=\frac{x-2}{2}e^{(x-4)/2}\). Hence describe the limiting position.

    [4]

  3. Find the time at which the particle reaches \(x=3\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v=12(2-x)/x\), initially on \(x\gt 2\).

(b)

The displayed relation holds with \(2\lt x\leq4\); \(x\to2^+\) as \(t\to\infty\).

(c)

\(t=1/12+(\ln2)/6\,\mathrm s\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Using \(a=v\,\mathrm dv/\mathrm dx\), integrate: \[v^2=-\frac{576}{x}+\frac{576}{x^2}+C.\] The initial data give \(36=-144+36+C\), so \(C=144\). Hence \[v^2=144\left(1-\frac2x\right)^2.\] Initially the particle moves left, and \(x\gt 2\). The appropriate branch is \[v=-12\left(1-\frac2x\right)=\frac{12(2-x)}x.\]

Part (b)

Separate the velocity equation: \[\mathrm dt=-\frac1{12}\left(1+\frac2{x-2}\right)\mathrm dx.\] Integrating from \(x=4,t=0\), \[12t=4-x-2\ln\frac{x-2}{2}.\] Rearrange and exponentiate: \[-6t=\frac{x-4}{2}+\ln\frac{x-2}{2},\qquad e^{-6t}=\frac{x-2}{2}e^{(x-4)/2}.\] On \(2\lt x\leq4\) the right side is positive and strictly increasing as a function of \(x\). As the left side decreases to zero, \(x\) decreases to 2. The logarithmic expression for time diverges as \(x\to2^+\), so this point is not reached at finite time.

Part (c)

Substitute \(x=3\) in the integrated relation: \[12t=1-2\ln\frac12=1+2\ln2.\] Therefore \(t=1/12+(\ln2)/6\). This is positive and finite, unlike the time to reach the limiting position \(x=2\).
questions.hint_html: After choosing the negative velocity branch, divide \(x/(x-2)\) into a constant plus a simple fraction.

Use the physical branch to justify the limiting position.
Substitute the target position in the valid implicit relation.

questions.title: Constant power opposed by quadratic resistance
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves forwards on a horizontal line. A driving force of magnitude \(108/v\) N acts forwards and a resistance of magnitude \(v^2/2\) N acts backwards. Its initial speed is \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and \(x=0\) initially.

  1. Find the speed as a function of displacement \(x\).

    [5]

  2. State the limiting speed and the power of the driving force.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(v=(216-189e^{-3x/4})^{1/3}\).

(b)

Limiting speed \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); driving power \(108\,\mathrm W\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Using \(a=v\,\mathrm dv/\mathrm dx\), Newton's law is \[2v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{108}{v}-\frac12v^2.\] Since \(v\gt 0\), multiply by \(v\): \[v^2\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=54-\frac14v^3.\] Let \(w=v^3\), so \(w'=3v^2v'\), with derivatives here taken with respect to \(x\). Then \[\frac{\mathrm dw}{\mathrm dx}=\frac34(216-w).\] This is separable. Integrating with \(w(0)=27\), \[216-w=189e^{-3x/4}.\] Thus \(v=(216-189e^{-3x/4})^{1/3}\). For \(x\geq0\), the quantity inside the root is at least 27, so the forward branch is well defined.

Part (b)

As \(x\to\infty\), \(v^3\to216\), so \(v\to6\). The driving power is force times speed: \[\mathcal P=\frac{108}{v}\,v=108\,\mathrm W.\] This interpretation applies on the positive-speed trajectory; the model's \(108/v\) force is not defined at rest.
questions.hint_html: Multiply the v–x equation by \(v\) so that \(v^2\,\mathrm dv\) can be integrated.

marking_criteria.description_html: Multiply by v and identify the v³ substitution.
Use force times velocity to find the driving power.

questions.title: A switched constant-power drive and a reachability threshold
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of mass \(m\) starts at \(O\) moving forwards at speed \(u\gt 0\) on a horizontal line. Initially the only horizontal force is resistance of magnitude \(mkv^2\), where \(k\gt 0\) and \(v\gt 0\) is speed.

At the instant the speed has fallen to \(u/3\), a forward force of magnitude \(mP/v\) is switched on and then remains active. The resistance is unchanged. The constant \(P\gt 0\) has units such that \(mP\) is the driving power.

  1. Find the distance travelled before the driving force is switched on.

    [3]

  2. Find the necessary and sufficient condition on \(P\) for the speed to return to \(u\) at a finite time after the switch. Explain the equality case.

    [3]

  3. Assume this condition holds. Find the total distance from \(O\) when the speed first returns to \(u\). Simplify your result when \(P=2ku^3\).

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(x_1=\ln3/k\).

(b)

\(P\gt ku^3\). At \(P=ku^3\), the speed approaches \(u\) but never reaches it at finite time.

(c)

\(x=\frac1{3k}\ln\frac{27P-ku^3}{P-ku^3}\); if \(P=2ku^3\), \(x=\ln53/(3k)\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Before the switch, \[v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=-kv^2.\] Since \(v\gt 0\), \(\mathrm dv/v=-k\,\mathrm dx\). Integrating from launch gives \(v=ue^{-kx}\). At \(v=u/3\), \[e^{-kx_1}=\frac13,\qquad x_1=\frac{\ln3}{k}.\]

Part (b)

After the switch, \[\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}=\frac Pv-kv^2.\] The positive equilibrium speed is \(V=(P/k)^{1/3}\). If \(P\gt ku^3\), the acceleration is positive and bounded away from zero on the compact speed interval \([u/3,u]\); consequently \(u\) is reached in finite time.

If \(ku^3/27\lt P\lt ku^3\), the speed increases but approaches a limit strictly below \(u\). For \(P\leq ku^3/27\), it does not initially accelerate from \(u/3\). Neither case reaches \(u\).

At \(P=ku^3\), the target is precisely the limiting speed. The separated time integrand \(v/(P-kv^3)\) has a logarithmic divergence as \(v\to u^-\). Thus equality must be excluded from the finite-time condition.

Part (c)

For the second stage, use the displacement equation: \[v\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dx}=\frac Pv-kv^2, \qquad \mathrm dx=\frac{v^2}{P-kv^3}\,\mathrm dv.\] Therefore the additional distance is \[x_2=\int_{u/3}^{u}\frac{v^2}{P-kv^3}\,\mathrm dv =\frac1{3k}\ln\frac{P-ku^3/27}{P-ku^3}.\] Both logarithm arguments are positive because \(P\gt ku^3\). Add the distance from part (a): \[x=x_1+x_2 =\frac1{3k}\ln\left(27\frac{P-ku^3/27}{P-ku^3}\right) =\frac1{3k}\ln\frac{27P-ku^3}{P-ku^3}.\] When \(P=2ku^3\), the ratio becomes \((54-1)/(2-1)=53\), giving \(x=\ln53/(3k)\). Integrating the post-switch law from the original launch would incorrectly omit the first stage.
questions.hint_html: Before the switch use \(\mathrm dv/v\); after it use \(v^2\,\mathrm dv/(P-kv^3)\). Check the sign of the latter denominator before integrating.
